name: Grant Park Guardian

location.address: Southeast entrance to Grant Park, E 11th Avenue at S Arthur Street, Spokane, WA 99202

official_register.name: Spokane Heritage Tree Register (City of Spokane Urban Forestry), 'Grant Park Guardian', CityandCountyHistoricProp FeatureServer layer 1

access: Free. Spokane city parks are open 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. (all city parks closed 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.). Tree stands at the park's southeast entrance.
transport: Street parking on E 11th Ave; Spokane Transit stops on the South Hill (route and walk time not checked)
story:
Heritage registers are usually dry reading. Spokane's gives this horse chestnut a job title: it calls the tree a guardian and greeter at the southeast entrance to Grant Park, and that is the name it goes by.

The job description fits. The register puts it at 75 feet, about 23 metres, on the park's East 11th Avenue edge. Horse chestnuts are a European species, not native to Washington, so this is a tree somebody chose for a park gate and the gate has kept it.

The city's listing gives its age as about 90. That figure was set when the tree was listed some years ago and nobody has re-measured since, so it is older now; somewhere from the mid-80s to past a century is the honest range. The register records no girth. If you have ever put a tape round it, tell us.

It was still standing in September 2025, when a naturalist logged a horse chestnut at the spot.

Come in May. That is when the tree carries its white flower candles upright over the whole crown, and a greeter at a gate earns its title. In autumn the conkers come down in their spiny cases. The park is free and open from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m., like every city park in Spokane, with street parking on East 11th.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the large horse chestnut right at the park's southeast entrance, 75 feet tall by the city register. It stands on the East 11th Avenue edge of Grant Park, near South Arthur Street.

best_time.label: May, when white candles stand upright over the whole crown

name: The Spokane Ponderosa

official_register.name: Spokane Heritage Tree Register (City of Spokane Urban Forestry), 'The Spokane Ponderosa'

access: Seen from the street in Browne's Addition; the register point sits beside an apartment building at 2028 W 2nd Ave, so the trunk may stand on private grounds. Pin the viewing place on the public sidewalk; do not invite anyone onto the property.
transport: Browne's Addition, west of downtown Spokane; Spokane Transit stops on W 2nd/Cannon area (route and walk time not checked)
verify_notes: One source (City of Spokane Heritage Tree Register, US one-source bar), flagged. Register text, whole: no age or height columns; description says it smells of vanilla (ponderosa bark), is the city's official tree species, 'growing nearly 200 feet tall' and 'the largest in the city', in the Browne's Addition Historic District. Do NOT repeat 200 ft as fact: it is the register's prose, not a measurement, and is implausible for an inland ponderosa (about 60 m; tallest ponderosas anywhere are roughly 70 m in California/Oregon old growth). Write 'the register calls it the largest in the city' only. Alive: iNaturalist obs 303180044 (Pinus ponderosa, 2025-08-02, 36 m accuracy, 10 m from the register point; CC BY-NC so not usable as a photo) confirms a ponderosa stands there. Spokane adopted the ponderosa as its official city tree (Spokesman-Review 2014-04-23, 'Ponderosa pine named Spokane's city tree'), good context. Context: a 130-year-old, about 120 ft Browne's Addition ponderosa fell in May 2019 and was cut up by the city (Spokesman-Review 2019-05-23, spokesman.com/stories/2019/may/23/city-cleans-up-130-year-old-fallen-tree-in-brownes); not shown to be this tree, so do not conflate, but it shows what neighbourhood ponderosas reach. Inlander 'To Be a Tree' says a Browne's Addition ponderosa may be the biggest in the municipal program (page rate-limited on fetch, only seen in search snippet, treat as pointer). No open photo found. No OSM natural=tree node (Overpass returned nothing).

name: The Last Planes of Browne's Addition

location.address: First Avenue near 2315 West 1st Avenue, Spokane, WA 99201 (street frontage by the Campbell House / Northwest Museum of Arts and Culture)

official_register.name: Spokane Heritage Tree Register (City of Spokane Urban Forestry), 'The Last Planes'

access: Free. Street trees along W 1st Avenue in the Browne's Addition Historic District, seen from the public sidewalk; the Campbell House museum grounds beside it are a separate paid visit.
transport: Browne's Addition, west of downtown Spokane; Spokane Transit stops nearby (route and walk time not checked)
verify_notes: One source (City of Spokane Heritage Tree Register), flagged. Register: 'a collection of three London planes' providing canopy along First Avenue in the Browne's Addition Historic District, age 110+, height about 65 feet (19.8 m, register figure), 'planted around the turn of the century', 'three remaining trees' that 'represent some of the original landscaping for this area of the neighborhood and, therefore, for the city'. The age is the register's at listing; add the years since. Alive: iNaturalist obs 268849116 (2025-04-05, 9 m accuracy, W First Ave, casual grade, genus only) at 47.656307,-117.446827, 3 m from the register point, shows a tree there; species not confirmed by it. Register point is address-level (2315 W 1st Ave) and sits at the Campbell House frontage; Commons files 3 to 27 m away show the house, not the planes. Three trees on one frontage is a compact ensemble with one place to stand, not an avenue; the writer should say a few planes along the frontage, not name individual trunks. Same address as the Reid Family Tree lead (private sugar maple, still a lead). Unrelated HistoryLink 10030 (Arksey 2012) notes the Browne's Addition variegated sycamore maple at the Campbell estate is the state's largest of its form, a possible different stop beside these planes (not this register's tree, no coordinate, not verified). No open photo.

name: The Rockwood Spruce

location.address: 725 East 26th Avenue, Spokane, WA 99203 (register address; point is beside 743 E 26th Ave)

official_register.name: Spokane Heritage Tree Register (City of Spokane Urban Forestry), 'The Rockwood Spruce'

access: Seen from East 26th Avenue in the Rockwood Historic District. It stands at a private house (register address 725 E 26th Ave): view from the public street only; pin the viewing place on the sidewalk, not the property.
transport: Rockwood, South Hill; Spokane Transit stops on Grand Blvd area (route and walk time not checked)
verify_notes: One source (City of Spokane Heritage Tree Register), flagged, and NOT confirmed alive: lifecheck returned NONE (no observation within range), so treat 'still standing' as unconfirmed until a dated photo or observation turns up. Register: Age 90+, height 125+ feet (38 m, register figure, plausible for Norway spruce), 'towering 125 feet above 26th Avenue', appears on the original 1926 landscaping plans of the Rockwood Historic District, designed by the Olmsted Brothers. Corroboration of the district context only: Wikipedia Rockwood Historic District and Rockwood, Spokane (Olmsted Brothers plan of 1910 with boulevards, medians and continuous street-tree rows); they do not mention this tree. The register's Towering Norwegian entry (Finch Arboretum, spk_011) says it is second-tallest of its kind in the city after a 'Brewton Spruce on 26th street'; probably this tree, but the register never links them, so say it only as the register's wording if at all. The 1926 landscaping plan date is a register claim; age shown as 90+ at listing. Walkable with nothing else verified; roughly 1.5 km from Grant Park Guardian (spk_015). No open photo. HistoryLink 10030 lists a Colorado spruce at 2105 Rockwood Boulevard (different tree).

name: The Corkscrew Willow of Liberty Park

location.address: West side of Liberty Park, Spokane, WA 99202

access: Free. Liberty Park is a city park, open 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. like all Spokane city parks.
transport: East Central Spokane; Spokane Transit stops near Liberty Park (route and walk time not checked)
verify_notes: One source (City of Spokane Heritage Tree Register, 'Liberty Park Champion'), flagged. Register: height 45 feet (13.7 m), diameter 50 inches, crown 60 feet, 'found on the west side of Liberty Park', 'likely the largest or second largest in the state' (the register's wording, hedged; no champion-list source seen). girth_cm 399 is DERIVED: 50 in = 127 cm diameter x pi, so a roughly 4 m circumference; plausible for a multi-stem old corkscrew willow but the register does not say where or whether the diameter is a single trunk (treat as register diameter, say so). No age in the register; corkscrew willow is short-lived, so do not infer one. Position is park-level (point inside Liberty Park per OSM, west side per register): approximate. Alive: lifecheck RECENT only because of an unrelated observation (iNat 307549145 nearby is a cottonwood); nothing observed of the willow itself, so alive is the register's say-so only, weaker than the other three. No open photo.
